lessons.title: Reported speech
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Change statements, questions and commands from direct to reported speech.
Apply the backshift of tenses and the changes of pronouns and time words.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Direct speech** gives the speaker's exact words: *Ada said, "I am tired."* **Reported (indirect) speech** tells what was said without quoting: *Ada said that she was tired.* There are no inverted commas, and the tense, pronouns and time words usually change.

blocks.title: Backshift of tenses
blocks.md:
When the reporting verb is in the **past** (*said, told, asked*), the tense moves **one step back**:
- present simple → past simple: *"I work"* → *he said he worked*
- present continuous → past continuous
- present perfect and simple past → **past perfect** (*had worked*)
- will → **would**; can → **could**; may → **might**; must → **had to**.
If the statement is a permanent truth, the tense may stay the same.

blocks.title: Other changes
blocks.md:
- **Pronouns** follow the sense: *"I"* → he/she, *"my"* → his/her, *"we"* → they.
- **Time and place:** now → *then*; today → *that day*; tomorrow → *the next day*; yesterday → *the day before*; here → *there*; this → *that*.
- **Questions:** no question mark, statement order, **if/whether** for yes/no questions: *"Are you ready?"* → *She asked if I was ready.*
- **Commands:** *told / asked + to-infinitive*: *"Sit down!"* → *He told us to sit down.*

blocks.caption: Shift one step back into the past.
blocks.alt: A table showing backshift: am is are become was were; go goes become went; have gone or went become had gone; will and can become would and could.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Keeping the question mark and the question order: *She asked where was I* → **She asked where I was.**
- *He said me that...* → **He told me that...** (told + person) or **He said that...**
- Forgetting to change time words: *tomorrow* → *the next day*.
- Keeping *I/my* instead of changing the pronoun.
- Leaving the inverted commas.

blocks.title: Example 1: a statement
blocks.statement: Report: *Ngu said, "I am going to the market tomorrow."*
steps: I → he; am going → **was going**; tomorrow → **the next day**.
No inverted commas and add *that* if you like.
blocks.answer: Ngu said that he was going to the market the next day.

blocks.title: Example 2: a question
blocks.statement: Report: *The teacher asked, "Have you finished your homework?"*
steps: Yes/no question → *if/whether*; present perfect → **past perfect**; you → **we** or **I** depending on the listener.
Use statement order and no question mark.
blocks.answer: The teacher asked if we had finished our homework.

lessons.title: The passive voice
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Form the passive in common tenses.
Decide when the passive is a good choice.
Change active sentences to passive and back.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: In an **active** sentence the subject does the action: *The farmers harvested the cocoa.* In a **passive** sentence the thing that receives the action becomes the subject: *The cocoa was harvested (by the farmers).* We use the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when we want to put the focus on the receiver.

blocks.title: Forming the passive
blocks.md:
**be (in the same tense) + past participle**:
- present simple: *The letter is written.*
- present continuous: *The road is being repaired.*
- simple past: *The match was cancelled.*
- present perfect: *The window has been broken.*
- future: *The results will be announced.*
- modals: *The work must be finished. Water can be purified.*
The doer (**agent**) comes after **by** and is often left out.

items.text: Active to passive: the roles swap

blocks.caption: The object moves to the front; the verb becomes be + participle.
blocks.alt: Two rows of boxes: the active row has subject, verb and object; the passive row has object, be plus past participle, and by plus subject, with an arrow from the verb to the be plus participle box.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the participle: *The cocoa was harvest* → **harvested**.
- Wrong tense of *be*: *The road is repaired now* (continuous: **is being repaired**).
- Only **transitive** verbs (verbs with an object) have a passive: *arrive, happen, die, go* do not (*The accident was happened* is wrong).
- Writing *by* + a pronoun in the wrong form: *by him / by them*, not *by he*.
- Overusing the passive in stories: it makes writing heavy.

blocks.title: Example 1: active to passive
blocks.statement: Rewrite in the passive: *The workers repaired the bridge last month.*
steps: Object *the bridge* becomes the subject; simple past → **was repaired**.
The agent is optional: *by the workers*.
blocks.answer: The bridge was repaired (by the workers) last month.

blocks.title: Example 2: passive to active
blocks.statement: Rewrite in the active: *The letters will be delivered by the postman tomorrow.*
steps: The doer is *the postman*: he becomes the subject.
Future passive *will be delivered* becomes active *will deliver*.
blocks.answer: The postman will deliver the letters tomorrow.

lessons.title: Conditional sentences and relative clauses
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Form zero, first, second and third conditionals.
Use who, which, whose, that and where in relative clauses.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **conditional sentence** has an *if* clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). The tense pattern shows how real or unreal the condition is. A **relative clause** gives more information about a noun.

blocks.title: Four conditionals
blocks.md:
- **Zero** (general truth): *If you heat ice, it melts.* (if + present, present)
- **First** (real, possible): *If it rains, we will stay at home.* (if + present, will + verb)
- **Second** (unreal or unlikely now): *If I were rich, I would build a hospital.* (if + past, would + verb; use **were** for all persons)
- **Third** (impossible, past): *If she had studied, she would have passed.* (if + past perfect, would have + participle)
**Unless** = *if not*: *Unless you hurry, you will be late.*

blocks.title: Relative clauses
blocks.md:
- **who** (people), **which** (things), **whose** (ownership), **where** (places), **that** (people or things, defining only).
- **Defining clause** (needed to know which one): no commas: *The boy who sits behind me is my cousin.*
- **Non-defining clause** (extra information): between commas, no *that*: *Mount Cameroon, which is in the South West, is often cloudy.*

blocks.caption: The tense in the if clause moves back as the condition becomes less real.
blocks.alt: A table of conditional patterns: first conditional present then will plus verb; second past then would plus verb; third past perfect then would have plus participle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *If it will rain, we will stay* → **If it rains**, we will stay.
- *If I was you* is often used in speech, but in writing use **If I were you**.
- *If he would have come* → **If he had come**.
- *The girl which sings* → **who** sings.
- Commas missing around a non-defining clause, or added to a defining one.

blocks.title: Example 1: choose the type
blocks.statement: Complete: *If I ___ (be) the Minister, I ___ (build) more schools.*
steps: This is an unreal, imaginary situation: second conditional.
if + past (were) and would + base verb.
blocks.answer: If I were the Minister, I would build more schools.

blocks.title: Example 2: join with a relative clause
blocks.statement: Combine: *Mount Cameroon is the highest peak in the region. It is in the South West.* (non-defining)
steps: The second sentence is extra information about Mount Cameroon: use *which* with commas.
blocks.answer: Mount Cameroon, which is in the South West, is the highest peak in the region.
